title: ▶︎Greene residents question ICE involvement with GCSO at BOS meeting - NewsBreak
text:
10 hours ago Kelly Marquis questioned whether Greene County Sheriff Steve Smith and his deputies were using racial profiling in selecting which vehicles to stop during a recent joint operation with federal ICE agents. PJR photo and video by Chuck Jackson.
Kelly Marquis questioned Greene County Sheriff Steve Smith and his deputies working with ICE to round up 26 county residents in recent weeks at Tuesday evening’s board of supervisors meeting.
The sheriff has been a proponent of Homeland Security’s 287(g) program where local law enforcement cooperates with its federal partners in apprehending suspected illegal aliens before handing them off to ICE agents.
In 2026, the sheriff received more than $350,000 from the federal government for their assistance.
Marquis questioned whether the deputies were using racial profiling in making random stops.
“If deputies are conducting stops that lead to immigration enforcement, what criteria is being used?” she asked. “Are they being targeted because they are suspected of serious criminal activity or undocumented or disabled Latinos?”
Melanie Johnson of Barboursville, informed supervisors her neighbor and his father were picked up by deputies along a county road, turned over to ICE, and taken to a Farmville detention center.
The son has lived in the county for 16 years, had a successful business, owned his own home, and now a wife is trying to raise two American-born children on her own.
“They don’t know if they’ll ever see their father again or their grandfather, who self-deported back to Mexico shortly after being detained,” Johnson added.
Ken Copeland of Standardsville, reiterated the previous speakers regarding the lack of transparency between the citizens of the county and Sheriff Smith.
Copeland also spoke at the May 26 BOS meeting.
“Transparency is needed,” Copeland stated. “You can hear there’s a lot of concern; a lot of harm being done with information that allows for public discussion. So, I would encourage you to encourage the sheriff to provide information mentioned earlier; what information should be provided.
“I know I would not want Greene County to be on the wrong side of history as has happened so many times in the past.”
While the speakers spoke, about 35 people stood in solidarity, with some holding signs aloft.
Johnson admitted she knew the BOS members couldn’t tell the sheriff what to do since he’s a constitutional officer not subject to the county’s oversight.
But Johnson said the board did have a financial hold on Sheriff Smith – should they wish to do so.
“W e’re here, all of us, standing, to demand that you stop enabling ICE collaboration in Greene County,” Johnson said. “Because what you have allowed through your budgetary approvals and your consent agenda appropriations have directly expanded the sheriff’s ability to collaborate with ICE. Those decisions are tearing families apart, undermining public safety and terrorizing this community.”
Since January, the supervisors have approved a total of $352,419 from Homeland Security to be placed in the sheriff’s budget.
“That’s not neutrality; that’s participation,” Johnson concluded.
Sheriff Smith, with arms folded across his chest, sat quietly in the back of the meeting room.
GCSO Major Josh White sat next to him while Captain Brian Shifflett, and a deputy stood outside the room keeping the peace.
Asked about the raids and Tuesday night’s meeting, the sheriff replied, “No comment.”
